title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Iterative radix-2 divider + single shared 33x33 multiplier to remove the 200 ns combinational DIV/REM path
motivation:
Baseline Fmax is 5.442 MHz. The worst path (199.8 ns, 156 cells) is
clock -> u_fwd -> u_ex -> u_ex/u_alu -> u_ex: the forwarding mux feeding
the fully combinational 32-bit `/` and `%` operators in alu.sv (four of
them: signed/unsigned div and rem, each ~32 cascaded 32-bit subtract
stages). Every other path in this 5-stage pipeline (forward mux, 32-bit
add/compare, redirect -> PC, decode) is an order of magnitude shorter,
so Fmax is set almost entirely by an operation that is essentially absent
from CoreMark's timed region (-O3 turns divide-by-constant into
multiply-high; the timed kernels contain no or only a handful of runtime
DIV/REM). The ALU also instantiates three separate 32x32->64
multipliers (ss, uu, su), tripling DSP/LUT usage and widening the
ALU result mux. LUT count (12312) is dominated by these units.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
1) Remove DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU from the combinational ALU and implement them
   in a new rtl/divider.sv: a classic 1-bit-per-cycle restoring (shift /
   subtract) divider on absolute values (~33-34 cycles per op), with
   operands latched on the start cycle from the *post-forward* rs1/rs2
   values in EX. Sign fix-up at the end (negate quotient if signs differ,
   remainder takes dividend sign). Special cases handled explicitly:
   divide-by-zero -> quotient all-ones / remainder = dividend (signed and
   unsigned); INT_MIN / -1 falls out correctly of the abs-value algorithm
   (q = 0x80000000, r = 0) but may also be special-cased for clarity.
   FSM: IDLE -> BUSY(count) -> DONE; DONE holds the result until the EX/MEM
   register actually advances (i.e. not during a dmem stall), then returns
   to IDLE so a back-to-back DIV in the next ID/EX restarts cleanly.
2) Pipeline control: new `div_stall` = (ID/EX is a valid DIV-class op) &&
   !div_done. hazard_unit ORs it into stall_if and stall_id (PC and ID/EX
   hold; flush_id must not bubble the DIV). The EX/MEM register captures a
   bubble (valid=0, reg_write=0, mem_read/mem_write=0) while div_stall &&
   !dmem_stall; dmem_stall keeps priority (EX/MEM holds). Because the
   older producers drain out of EX/MEM and MEM/WB during the stall, the
   EX/MEM rs1_val/rs2_val/write_data for the DIV on its completion cycle
   come from the divider's latched operand copies, not the (now stale)
   forward muxes. A DIV never redirects, so no interaction with redirect.
3) Replace the three multipliers with ONE signed 33x33 multiply:
   a_ext = {a_signed & a[31], a}, b_ext = {b_signed & b[31], b} where
   MULH: both signed, MULHSU: a signed only, MULHU/MUL: unsigned. MUL
   takes prod[31:0], MULH* take prod[63:32]. 33x33 maps onto one Gowin
   MULT36X36 (or 4x MULT18X18) instead of three, shrinking area and the
   result mux. MUL stays single-cycle in EX (no IPC change for matrix
   kernels).
4) Formal / ALTOPS: under `RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` keep the exact same
   substitution formulas for all eight M ops (DIV-class computed from the
   latched operands inside divider.sv, or from the ALU as today), but make
   the divider's latency short under ALTOPS (e.g. complete after 1-2
   cycles) so the stall/handshake path is still exercised while staying
   well inside the riscv-formal BMC depth and liveness bound. The
   non-ALTOPS path is the real iterative divider.
Expected result: the critical path drops from ~200 ns to the
forward-mux -> multiplier/adder/branch-compare -> EX/MEM or redirect -> PC
paths, roughly 20-30 ns, i.e. Fmax ~35-50 MHz (6-9x). CPI cost is
~33 cycles per runtime DIV/REM, which is negligible in CoreMark's timed
region, so iter/s should rise by several hundred percent (capped at +50
in the schema field below). LUT usage should also drop substantially,
easing placement.

changes.description: New module: 1-bit/cycle restoring divider for DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU with IDLE/BUSY/DONE FSM, start/advance handshake, latched post-forward operands (also exported for RVFI rs1/rs2 values), abs-value + sign fix-up, explicit divide-by-zero handling, and short-latency ALTOPS substitution under `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS`.

Delete the combinational `/` and `%` arms (DIV-class ops default to 0 / unused from ALU). Replace mul_ss/mul_uu/mul_su with a single signed 33x33 product using op-dependent sign extension; MUL=prod[31:0], MULH/MULHSU/MULHU=prod[63:32]. Keep the ALTOPS branch for MUL-class ops identical.

Instantiate divider; start it when a valid DIV-class op sits in ID/EX and the unit is IDLE; export div_stall to the hazard unit; select divider result into alu_result on completion; while div_stall && !stall (dmem) capture a bubble into EX/MEM; on completion use the divider's latched operands for rs1_val/rs2_val/write_data.
Add div_stall input; OR it into stall_if and stall_id; ensure flush_id does not bubble ID/EX while the DIV is waiting; keep dmem_stall priority for EX/MEM hold.
Wire div_stall between ex_stage and hazard_unit.
Optional helper (e.g. is_div flag in ctrl_t or decode of alu_op range ALU_DIV..ALU_REMU) for cheap DIV-class detection in EX.

Keep all MUL/MULH/MULHSU/MULHU vectors (add a few more MULH/MULHSU sign-corner vectors to cover the new shared 33x33 multiplier). Remove only the combinational DIV/REM checks, which move to test_divider.py.

New clocked cocotb suite for divider.sv: every DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU vector previously in test_alu.py (incl. divide-by-zero, INT_MIN/-1, back-to-back divides) plus randomized vectors checked against Python reference semantics; start pulse, wait for done, check exact result, verify result holds in DONE until advance. No vector is dropped.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-001-r1s0 (regression, +721.45%): Moving the combinational `/`/`%` into an iterative radix-2 divider with a div_stall is what delivers the ~8x fitness gain (CoreMark barely executes runtime DIV/REM); this variant kept MUL single-cycle via one shared 33x33 signed multiply and scored within ~0.4% of the same-round sibling that also made MUL multi-cycle, so after the divider fix, single-cycle shared MUL vs pipelined MUL is a wash and the "regression" label reflects only the sibling landing first.

title: Move MUL/DIV out of single-cycle EX: multi-cycle M-unit (pipelined DSP multiplier + iterative radix-2 divider) with EX-stage stall
motivation:
The baseline Fmax is 5.44 MHz because the EX stage evaluates a fully
combinational 32-bit divider/remainder (plus three separate 32x32->64
multipliers) in one cycle. The logged critical path is 199.8 ns / 150
logic levels through cpu/u_fwd -> cpu/u_ex -> cpu/u_ex/u_alu -> dmem,
i.e. forwarding mux -> ALU (DIV/REM array) -> EX/MEM result that Gowin
absorbs into the dmem BSRAM address register. Every other path in the
5-stage pipe is roughly 10x shorter. CoreMark -O3 executes very few
DIV/REM and a modest number of MULs, so paying a few extra cycles on
those instructions in exchange for removing the deep array from the
single-cycle path is an overwhelming win: fitness = iter/cycle x Fmax,
and Fmax should rise by ~8-12x while iter/cycle drops by only a few %.
The 12.3k LUT4 count (well over the 10k target) is also dominated by the
combinational divider, so area drops sharply too.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure the EX stage so the M-extension is executed by a separate
multi-cycle unit (rtl/muldiv.sv) that stalls the front of the pipeline
while it works, and strip all `*`, `/`, `%` out of the single-cycle ALU.

1. rtl/muldiv.sv (new). Start/busy/done handshake, operands latched on
   the start cycle.
   - Multiplier: ONE 33x33 signed multiply instead of three 64-bit ones.
     Operands are sign- or zero-extended to 33 bits per op (MUL/MULHU:
     zero/zero; MULH: sign/sign; MULHSU: sign/zero). Pipeline it so it
     maps onto Gowin DSP blocks with registered inputs and registered
     product: cycle 0 latch extended operands into regs, cycle 1
     product register (a_q * b_q), cycle 2 select [31:0] or [63:32]
     into a result register. Total ~3 cycles per MUL*, no carry chain
     or LUT adder tree on any single-cycle path.
   - Divider: iterative radix-2 restoring (or non-restoring) divider,
     1 quotient bit/cycle, 32 iterations on |a|, |b| with a 33-bit
     subtract per cycle, then sign-fix of quotient/remainder into the
     result register (~34 cycles). Special cases handled on the start
     cycle with an immediate done (no iteration): divisor==0 -> q=all
     ones, r=dividend; INT_MIN / -1 -> q=INT_MIN, r=0. Keep the RV32M
     sign rules exactly as in the current alu.sv comments (remainder
     takes the sign of the dividend).
   - `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS: result = the same ALTOPS formulas
     currently in alu.sv ((a+b)^const / (a-b)^const per op), computed
     from the latched operands, and ALL M-ops use a SHORT fixed latency
     (2-3 cycles). This keeps the stall/forwarding/handshake logic under
     formal while staying inside the 20-step liveness/insn BMC depth (a
     34-cycle divider would blow the liveness depth). The real path
     (`else) is the one Verilator/cosim/FPGA use.
2. rtl/alu.sv: delete the three 64-bit multipliers and the DIV/REM
   logic (and their ALTOPS arms); the ALU becomes add/sub/logic/shift/
   compare/LUI only. The M-op encodings in core_pkg stay; the decoder
   additionally sets a new ctrl bit `is_muldiv` for funct7=0000001.
3. EX-stage control (ex_stage.sv, hazard_unit.sv, core.sv):
   - m_start = ID/EX valid && ctrl.is_muldiv && unit idle && !done.
     Operand values are taken from the post-forwarding rs1/rs2 on the
     FIRST cycle the instruction sits in EX (forwarding is guaranteed
     valid then; load-use already inserted its bubble). They MUST be
     latched: while the M-op waits, older instructions drain out of
     EX/MEM and MEM/WB so the forwarding sources disappear and
     ID/EX.rs?_val may be stale.
   - m_stall = ID/EX holds an M-op that is not yet done. On m_stall:
     PC holds (stall_if), ID/EX HOLDS (stall_id=1, flush_id=0 — not a
     bubble), and the EX/MEM register captures a BUBBLE (valid=0,
     reg_write=0, mem_read=mem_write=0) so older instructions keep
     draining through MEM/WB. dmem_stall keeps priority (EX/MEM and
     everything upstream hold; the M-unit may keep iterating since its
     operands are latched; `done` is sticky until the op leaves EX).
   - On the done cycle the op advances normally: EX/MEM.alu_result =
     m_result_q (a registered value, so the only new logic on the hot
     EX path is one extra mux input on alu_result); the unit returns to
     idle when the op leaves EX (not dmem-stalled), so back-to-back
     M-ops each start fresh.
   - RVFI: EX/MEM.rs1_val/rs2_val for an M-op come from the unit's
     latched raw operands (not the possibly-stale forwarding muxes).
     These fields are RVFI-only and pruned by synthesis.
   - An M-op in EX can never be flushed (redirects originate in EX and
     M-ops never redirect), so no kill path is needed; reset clears the
     unit.
Expected result: the worst path collapses from ~200 ns to the normal
5-stage paths (forward mux -> 32-bit add/compare -> redirect/PC or dmem
address), roughly 15-25 ns on GW2A => Fmax ~40-65 MHz. CPI cost: ~2-3
extra cycles per MUL and ~33 per DIV/REM; CoreMark's inner loops are
dominated by loads/branches/ALU ops, so iter/cycle should fall by only
a few percent. LUT4 count should drop by several thousand.

title: 64-entry BTB with 2-bit counters in IF: zero-bubble taken branches/jumps
motivation:
The core has no prediction: every taken branch, JAL and JALR resolves in EX
and flushes the two younger slots (IF + ID), a 2-cycle penalty. RV32IM -O3
CoreMark runs about 16-18% conditional branches, with roughly 55-60% of them
taken (loop back-edges in list/matrix/crc/state loops), plus about 3% JAL/JALR.
That is about 0.12-0.13 taken control transfers per instruction, or about
0.25 CPI of about 1.65 total (4.49M cycles per 10 iterations).
The 22% imem stalls hide part of that penalty, because a stalled wrong-path
fetch costs nothing extra. Even so, the effective penalty is still about
1.5 cycles per taken transfer.
Fmax is 5.44 MHz. The limit is the combinational divider path
(u_mem.rd -> u_fwd -> u_ex -> u_alu -> EX/MEM, 150 logic levels, 200 ns).
So a predictor lookup in IF (PC reg -> small LUT-RAM -> next-PC mux, about 10
levels) and a mispredict compare in EX (about 5 more levels on the
non-divider branch path) are far off the critical path. The IPC gain should
carry over almost fully to fitness, with no Fmax loss.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a direct-mapped 64-entry branch target buffer (BTB) with a per-entry
2-bit saturating counter, looked up combinationally from the IF PC register.
Branch resolution moves from "redirect on every taken branch" to "redirect
only on mispredict". EX stays the only resolution point.

BTB organisation (inside if_stage.sv so no new source file is needed; the
cocotb test_pipeline source list is explicit):
  - index = pc[7:2] (64 entries), tag = pc[15:8] (8 bits), target = pc[31:2]
    (30 bits), ctr = 2 bits. Declare the tag, target and ctr arrays as
    reset-less `logic [N:0] arr [0:63]` with one synchronous write port and
    one async read, so Gowin maps them to LUT-RAM (SSRAM). Hold the
    valid bits in a 64-bit flop vector with synchronous reset. The prediction
    is therefore well defined from reset for cosim and formal. Any stale or
    aliased entry is only a prediction and is always checked in EX.
  - predict_taken = valid[idx] && tag match && ctr[1].
    next_pc = predict_taken ? {target,2'b00} : pc+4. Redirect keeps priority
    over stall, and PC only advances when !stall, as today. imem stall and
    load-use stall therefore just re-look-up the same PC next cycle.
  - IF->ID bundle (if_id_t) and ID/EX (id_ex_t) gain: pred_taken (1),
    pred_target (32), pred_hit (1), pred_ctr (2). When the IF output is a
    bubble (flush || redirect || imem stall), force pred_taken = 0 and
    pred_hit = 0. Otherwise an imem-stall NOP, which carries pc = the
    held PC, would "mispredict" to pc+4 and skip a real instruction. ID/EX
    flush/reset zeroes them as it does every other field.

EX-stage resolution (ex_stage.sv):
  - actual_redirecting = (branch_taken || is_jump) && !misalign_fault
    (the current `redirect` expression). actual_target = the current
    redirect_target.
  - mispredict = in.valid && ( pred_taken ? (!actual_redirecting ||
    pred_target != actual_target) : actual_redirecting ).
  - redirect = mispredict. redirect_target = actual_redirecting ?
    actual_target : in.pc + 4. This equals the pc_next already computed for
    RVFI, so pc_wdata/pc_fwd semantics are unchanged. Non-control
    instructions that were falsely predicted taken (aliasing) redirect back
    to pc+4. A misaligned-target trap redirects to pc+4.
  - BTB update (write port driven from EX, registered write). Condition:
    in.valid && (is_branch || is_jump) && !misalign_fault && !stall_ex_mem.
    The dmem-stall gate is essential: EX holds for several cycles on a dmem
    stall and must not bump the counter repeatedly.
      taken/jump: write tag, target=actual_target, valid=1,
        ctr = pred_hit ? sat_inc(pred_ctr) : (is_jump ? 2'b11 : 2'b10)
      not-taken branch with pred_hit: ctr = sat_dec(pred_ctr) (rewrite the
        same tag/target from pred_target, or use a separate ctr-only write)
      not-taken branch without hit: no allocation.
    pred_ctr/pred_hit ride down the pipe, so the BTB needs only one read port
    (IF) and one write port (EX).
  - Everything else stays as it is: the redirect flushes (IF NOP + ID/EX
    bubble via the existing hazard_unit flush_if/flush_id logic, with its
    dmem_stall precedence), the forwarding, the load-use stall, the
    RVFI/pc_next, and the divider.
    No valid instruction in EX is ever wrong-path, because every redirect
    flushes both younger slots. The BTB is therefore only trained by
    architecturally correct instructions.

Expected effect: a BTB with 2-bit counters reaches about 85-90% accuracy on
CoreMark's loop-dominated branches and correctly predicts direct JALs and
single-caller returns. Correctly predicted taken transfers go from about 1.5
effective penalty cycles to 0. Branches predicted taken that fall through
now cost 2 cycles; they are rare with 2-bit hysteresis. Net saving is about
0.13-0.18 CPI of about 1.65, so iterations/cycle should rise by about 8-11%.
Fmax stays divider-bound at about 5.4 MHz.
The predictor adds about 64 FFs plus about 45 bits x 64 of LUT-RAM plus about
150-250 LUTs. None of it is in the divider cone.

Correctness guards for the implementer:
  - Run test_pipeline (branches/JAL/JALR/load-use/forwarding),
    cosim with --istall --dstall, and formal (pc_fwd/pc_bwd, unique,
    liveness, ill).
  - The riscv-formal liveness check still holds: every mispredict still
    retires the EX instruction and redirects to its true successor.
  - Do NOT touch alu.sv, mul/div or the ALTOPS block.

changes.description: Add the 64-entry direct-mapped BTB (LUT-RAM tag/target/ctr arrays, reset flop valid vector), combinational lookup from pc, next_pc = predicted target when hit && ctr[1]. Add BTB write-port inputs driven from EX. Emit pred_taken/pred_target/pred_hit/pred_ctr in the IF->ID bundle, forced to 0 on flush/redirect/imem-stall bubbles.
Extend if_id_t and id_ex_t with pred_taken, pred_target[31:0], pred_hit, pred_ctr[1:0].

title: Shrink the EX-redirect cone: no NOP-mux/load-use on redirect, ID/EX squash clears only valid+ctrl
motivation:
The champion's worst path (27.0 ns, 19 logic levels, -16.7 ns slack) is
u_rf -> u_id (ID/EX rs1_val) -> u_ex (fwd mux + branch compare ->
redirect) -> u_if (instr = (flush||redirect) ? NOP : imem_data) ->
u_hazard (load-use rs1/rs2 == id_ex.rd compare -> stall_id/flush_id) ->
u_id (CE/clear of the ~250-bit ID/EX register, endpoint
id_ex_w.rs1_val_0_s100). The same redirect->NOP mux also feeds the
regfile read addresses and decoder/imm_gen that form the ID/EX D-inputs.
Every one of those redirect uses is redundant: (a) hazard_unit already
asserts flush_id on redirect, so the NOP substitution in IF buys nothing;
(b) load_use_hazard needs a LOAD in EX while redirect needs a
branch/jump in EX, so the two are mutually exclusive and the load-use
detector never needs to see the squashed instruction; (c) only valid and
the ctrl bundle of a squashed ID/EX entry have any architectural effect
(every consumer of pc/rs*_val/imm/rd/rs*_addr/instr is gated by
valid or by ctrl bits), so the late redirect need not fan out to the
data fields at all.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Two coupled changes that leave cycle-level behaviour identical (same
CoreMark cycle count) but pull `redirect` out of the ID-stage cone:
1. if_stage: out.instr = imem_ready ? imem_data : NOP and
   out.valid = imem_ready. No redirect/flush term. imem_ready and
   imem_data are flip-flop outputs in the timed bench (LFSR +
   bench_stall_gen), so this mux is early. The hazard unit's rs1/rs2
   and the regfile read addresses therefore depend only on early
   signals; load-use detection becomes independent of the EX compare.
2. id_stage ID/EX register split: valid + ctrl (~27 FFs) clear on
   reset || flush and otherwise load when !stall; all data fields
   (pc, rs1_val, rs2_val, imm, rd, rs1_addr, rs2_addr, instr) load
   when !stall and ignore flush (reset kept). stall_id no longer has a
   redirect term, so the ~220 data FFs' CE is redirect-free and the
   critical redirect net fans out only to the PC mux and ~27 ctrl/valid
   flops.

redirect -> 1 LUT -> ctrl/PC FFs, dropping the u_if mux, the 5-bit
compare pair + OR in u_hazard, the stall/CE LUT and the 250-fanout net
(~4-5 levels + heavy routing, est. 27 ns -> 21-23 ns, +15-25% Fmax).

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-001-r2s0 (regression, +38.85%): The late EX redirect was mostly driving redundant logic (the IF NOP mux feeding regfile addresses/decode, the load-use rs1/rs2 compare, and the flush/CE of the ~220 ID/EX data flops), so making IF's NOP depend only on imem_ready and letting flush clear just ID/EX valid+ctrl (data fields load on !stall only, safe because every consumer is gated by valid/ctrl and load-use and redirect can't both fire) kept cycle behaviour unchanged by design and lifted fitness 99.94 -> 138.77, beating the +22% prediction (~65 MHz implied vs a one-seed 58.8 MHz pre-measure); the "regression" label is therefore not a loss vs the champion, and pruning the fan-out of late control signals to only valid/ctrl flops is a cheap, IPC-neutral Fmax lever.

title: Split control-flow redirect: ID-stage static redirect (JAL + backward branches) and a registered EX mispredict redirect
motivation:
After the muldiv fix the champion runs at 46.8 MHz. Its critical path is
27.0 ns over 19-21 logic levels, the same on every seed:
  ID/EX (rs1_val / rd / ctrl) -> u_fwd select -> 3:1 forward mux ->
  32-bit branch compare / rs1+imm JALR adder (u_ex) -> `redirect` ->
  u_if NOP-mux of the IF/ID instruction -> u_hazard load-use compare
  (if_id_rs1/rs2) -> stall_id / flush_id -> u_id ID/EX enable/clear
  (ends at id_ex_w.rs1_val).
Measured Gowin breakdown (make timing, place option 0, path 1):
  - clock insertion 5.3 ns;
  - regfile BSRAM (u_rf/regs_regs_0_0_s, its registered output is
    effectively ID/EX.rs*_val) clock-to-out done at 7.6 ns;
  - ID hold mux and 2-level forward mux done at 11.7 ns;
  - 32-bit compare carry chain done at 14.2 ns (EX is finished here);
  - then ~13 ns of control fan-out: redirect -> u_if n330
    (flush/NOP-mux, fanout 104) at 18.2 ns -> rs2_addr_w (the NOP-muxed
    rs field, which is also the regfile BSRAM read address) at 19.6 ns
    -> u_hazard load-use carry compare at 21.6 ns -> 3 u_id stall/flush
    LUTs (fanout 33) -> id_ex rs1_val flop at 27.0 ns.
  - Every one of the top 25 setup paths is this chain, into id_ex
    rs1/rs2_val or u_if/pc.
Registering the redirect cuts the chain at ~14.5 ns arrival. That is
~9 ns of launch-to-capture versus ~21.7 ns today. The ALU ->
dmem-address path has a similar prefix plus a result mux, ~17-18 ns
arrival.
`redirect` is also the select of the 32-bit PC mux, and redirect_target
(forwarded rs1 + imm) feeds the PC register. Branch resolution is
chained combinationally into the next fetch and into the ID/EX clock
enable, so the path covers most of EX plus most of the front end.
Every other path in the core (ALU -> EX/MEM / dmem address, imem ->
decode -> regfile -> ID/EX, dmem -> load-align -> MEM/WB) is
roughly 10-13 levels. So cutting this one chain is the largest Fmax
gain on offer.
Just registering the redirect would add 1 cycle to every taken
transfer. The BTB experiment measured a ~7% cycle cost for taken
transfers today (4.49M -> 4.19M cycles). A plain registered redirect
would give back ~7% IPC. To avoid that, the easy transfers move to ID,
where they cost 0 cycles.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure where control flow is resolved. The core then has two
redirect sources, and neither sits on the EX compare path:

1. Front-end (ID) redirect, zero-bubble, static. IF/ID is
   combinational (PC reg -> imem_data -> decode -> ID/EX), so the
   instruction at the IF output is "in ID". A small pre-decoder on
   imem_data detects:
     - JAL, and
     - conditional BRANCH with a negative B-immediate (instr[31]=1),
       which is backward-taken-forward-not-taken (BTFN): loop back-edges.
   It computes id_target = pc + (is_jal ? J-imm : B-imm) with one
   dedicated 32-bit adder in if_stage. The redirect is gated by
   alignment (J-imm bit1 = instr[21], B-imm bit1 = instr[8] must be 0,
   so misaligned targets fall through and still trap in EX exactly as
   today), by !stall_if and by !redirect_q.
   When it fires: pc <= id_target. The JAL/branch itself still enters
   ID/EX this cycle, and nothing is flushed.
   With this gating, "instruction captured valid into ID/EX" is
   equivalent to "PC advanced through the front-end next-PC mux".
   So a JAL or predicted branch in ID/EX always had its redirect
   applied. A new ID/EX bit `pred_taken` records this.
   This path is short: imem_data (a register in the bench) -> opcode /
   imm-bit decode -> adder -> PC mux. The gate uses load_use,
   dmem_ready, m_stall and redirect_q, which are all from registers
   or shallow.
2. Back-end (EX) redirect, registered. EX still does the full branch
   compare and JALR add, but the result only feeds flops:
     mispredict = ex_valid && !misalign_fault &&
                  ( is_jalr || (is_branch && branch_taken != pred_taken) )
     fix_target = is_jalr ? {jalr_sum[31:1],0}
                : branch_taken ? branch_target : pc+4
     redirect_q        <= mispredict && !stall_ex_mem   (the resolving
                          instruction must actually move EX->MEM)
     redirect_target_q <= fix_target
   JAL never mispredicts because it always redirected in ID.
   On the cycle redirect_q=1:
     - PC <= redirect_target_q (highest priority after reset);
     - the IF output is NOP'd and ID/EX is cleared (flush_if / flush_id
       use redirect_q instead of the combinational redirect);
     - the single wrong-path instruction now in EX is squashed:
       ex_valid = in.valid && !redirect_q. This gates EX/MEM valid/ctrl
       (bubble), the muldiv start/is_mop/m_stall (a squashed M-op must
       never start the unit), and the mispredict logic itself.
   rvfi pc_next keeps its current formula (architectural next PC,
   pc+4 on misalign trap), so RVFI/pc_fwd semantics do not change.

Cycle accounting (current: every taken transfer = 1 bubble):
  JAL: 1 -> 0. Backward taken branch (loop back-edge): 1 -> 0.
  Backward not-taken (loop exit): 0 -> 2. Forward taken: 1 -> 2.
  Forward not-taken: 0 -> 0. JALR (ret / indirect): 1 -> 2.
CoreMark -O3 is dominated by rotated loops (crc, matrix, list walk)
whose back-edges are backward-taken, plus calls/`j`. The net CPI
change should be about 0 (between -3% and +4% cycles).
Fmax: the 19-21 level chain is gone. The new worst paths are:
  - EX ALU -> EX/MEM / dmem BSRAM address, about 11-13 levels;
  - EX forward -> compare -> redirect_q, which now ends at ~33 flops
    instead of fanning out to PC + ID/EX enables;
  - imem -> regfile/decode -> ID/EX.
Expect about 60-72 MHz, i.e. +30-50% Fmax. Net fitness gain should be
about +25-40%, well above the 4.6% acceptance bar.
Implementation must-keeps:
  - The regfile BSRAM read address (the IF/ID instruction's rs fields
    after the NOP-mux) and the load-use compare must depend only on
    registered flush sources (redirect_q, imem_ready). Never feed the
    ID-stage predictor or any EX signal into them.
  - The ID predictor's pred_taken bit going into ID/EX is the ungated
    decode. Only the PC-mux select is gated by stall_if / redirect_q.

title: Zero-bubble IF/ID-stage branch prediction (JAL + agree-BHT seeded by BTFN), mispredict-only EX redirect, redirect taken off the IF->hazard path
motivation:
Every taken branch, JAL and JALR resolves in EX and flushes the two younger
slots, a 2-cycle penalty. The earlier BTB attempt (hyp-20260930-003-r1s2)
is misread in LESSONS.md. Its cycle count fell from 4,491,485 to 4,186,330
(-6.8% cycles, +7.3% IPC). Its fitness gained only +2.97% because its Fmax
dropped from 5.44 to 5.23 MHz. So the taken-transfer penalty is worth about
7% of cycles on this pipeline, and it is still there in the champion
(4,680,666 cycles).
A BTB in IF is the wrong shape for this core. The core has no IF/ID
register: io_imemData, which is a register (the LFSR) in the timed bench,
is decoded in the same cycle the PC fetches it. A predictor that
pre-decodes the fetched word and computes pc+imm can therefore redirect the
PC on the very next edge. That gives a zero-bubble taken branch or JAL with
no tag or target storage. Only a tiny direction table indexed by the PC
register is needed, and it is read in parallel with the fetch.
The champion's critical path (27.0 ns, 19 levels) is ID/EX -> fwd mux ->
branch compare -> redirect -> if_stage NOP mux on out.instr -> hazard
load-use compare on if_id rs1/rs2 -> stall_id/flush_id -> ID/EX enable.
The redirect -> NOP-mux -> load-use leg is logically redundant, because a
redirect already bubbles ID/EX via flush_id and overrides the PC stall. The
predictor rework rewrites exactly this redirect/flush plumbing. We should
cut that leg in the same change, so that prediction is Fmax-positive and
not Fmax-negative (the lesson was that a predictor must cost < ~3% Fmax).

   imem_data and the PC register. Keep it in this file: test_pipeline.py has
   an explicit source list.
   - is_jal = opcode==1101111. is_br = opcode==1100011 && funct3 not in {2,3}.
     imm_j / imm_b are extracted locally, the same as imm_gen.
     pred_target = pc + (is_jal ? imm_j : imm_b).
   - Direction table: 64 x 2-bit counters in plain FLOPS (resettable, so
     cosim and formal are deterministic), indexed by pc[7:2]. It is an
     "agree" predictor. Counter MSB=1 means "agree with static BTFN", where
     BTFN = imm sign bit (instr[31]): backward = taken, forward = not taken.
     Reset all counters to 2'b10 (weakly agree). Cold behaviour is therefore
     BTFN, and the table learns forward-taken and backward-not-taken
     exceptions. dir = ctr[1] ? instr[31] : !instr[31].
   - pred_taken = imem_ready && (is_jal || (is_br && dir)) && imm[1]==0.
     Never predict a misaligned target. EX's existing misalign trap then
     sees an un-predicted instruction and suppresses the redirect as today.
   - PC update priority: reset > redirect(EX) > stall_if (hold) >
     pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4. The PC advances with the prediction
     exactly when ID/EX captures a valid instruction (!stall_if && !redirect),
     so the prediction and the instruction entering ID/EX stay paired.
   - IF->ID bundle gains pred_taken and pred_ctr[1:0]. out.instr/out.valid
     are muxed only by imem-not-ready (flush_if), NOT by redirect. ID/EX is
     already cleared by flush_id on redirect, and the PC takes the redirect
     over any stall.
   - A BHT write port (en, idx, next ctr) is driven from the EX/MEM REGISTER
     (update one cycle after resolution, so it is off the branch-compare path):
     en = ex_mem.valid && ex_mem.ctrl.is_branch && !stall_ex_mem,
     agree = (ex_mem.branch_taken == ex_mem.instr[31]), ctr' = saturating
     ctr +/- 1 using the pred_ctr carried down the pipe.
2. EX resolution becomes mispredict-only (ex_stage.sv):
     redirect = ( (is_branch && (branch_cond ^ pred_taken))
                || (is_jump && !is_jalr && !pred_taken)   // robustness only
                ||  is_jalr ) && !misalign_fault
     redirect_target = is_jalr ? jalr_target
                     : is_jump ? jal_target
                     : pred_taken ? pc+4 : branch_target
   The target select uses only ID/EX-register bits, so the branch_cond ->
   redirect depth is unchanged (AND becomes XOR). pc_next and all RVFI
   fields are unchanged, because they always report the architectural next
   PC. Correctly predicted JALs and taken branches no longer flush anything.
   A mispredicted branch costs 2 cycles, the same as a taken branch today.
   JALR keeps its 2-cycle penalty. A RAS is out of scope.
3. Critical-path relief that comes with the redirect rework:
   - hazard_unit load-use compares io_imemData[19:15]/[24:20] (raw fetch
     word) instead of the redirect-muxed if_id instr. flush_if = imem_stall
     only. This is equivalent: on redirect, the PC takes redirect_target
     regardless of stall_if, and ID/EX takes flush (flush beats stall in
     id_stage). On imem_stall, the PC holds and ID/EX captures a bubble
     either way (load_use also forces flush_id). With m_stall, id_ex
     mem_read=0, so load_use cannot fire. The redirect net then drives only
     the PC mux and the ID/EX flush, not the NOP mux -> 5-bit compares ->
     stall/flush chain.
   - id_stage flush clears only valid, ctrl and pred_* (reset still clears
     everything). This cuts redirect fanout from ~200 ID/EX flops to ~30.
     Data fields of an invalid, ctrl=0 entry are never consumed: forward
     and hazard are gated by ctrl.reg_write/mem_read, and RVFI by valid.
Expected: about 5-6.5% fewer cycles (JAL is fully free, BTFN + agree-BHT
covers most loop back-edges and biased forward branches, and there are no
cold-target misses as a BTB has). Fmax is flat to +10% from removing about
4-5 of the 19 levels from the champion's worst path. The new next-PC path
(LFSR reg -> opcode/imm pre-decode -> 30-bit add -> 2 muxes -> PC) is about
10 levels, well under the current worst path. Cost: about 130 FF (the BHT)
and about 200 LUT4.

title: Operand-path diet: regfile out of BSRAM into LUT-RAM + real ID/EX flops, registered 4:1 forward selects, AUIPC folded into ID, dedicated dmem AGU
motivation:
Gowin place-and-route of the champion (make timing, placement option 0:
60.7 MHz, 16.43 ns data path) shows that ALL 25 worst paths start at
cpu/u_rf/regs_regs_0_0_s. That cell is a BSRAM: GowinSynthesis took the
async-read reg_file together with the ID/EX rs1_val/rs2_val flops and mapped
them to a synchronous-read BSRAM. The ID/EX operand "register" is really the
BSRAM output (tC2Q = 2.26 ns) followed by 2 LUTs in u_id
(id_ex_w.rs1_val_*_s17/_s16, the retimed write-first bypass + stall hold).
The path then continues through:
  u_ex fwd mux, 3 LUT levels (rs1_*_s9/s8/s7)          ~2.35 ns
  alu_a = is_auipc ? pc : rs1, 1 LUT + 1.1 ns route    ~1.50 ns
  u_alu, 2 LUT levels                                  ~2.75 ns
  u_ex result/alu_result mux, 3 LUT levels (n701_*)    ~3.35 ns
  dmem address hold mux (dmem_addr_c_*)                ~1.47 ns
  route to the dmem BSRAM ADB (EX/MEM.alu_result is
  absorbed into the BSRAM address register)            ~1.23 ns
The next distinct start point is cpu/u_mem/reg_q.rd_3_s0 at -11.440 ns
slack vs -11.463 ns: the MEM/WB.rd -> forward-compare -> fwd mux path is
practically as long. Fixing only the regfile would therefore gain nothing
unless the forwarding compare also leaves the EX path.
Past lessons say pruning late-signal logic is a cheap, IPC-neutral Fmax
lever (r2s0: +38.85%). This hypothesis applies the same idea to the
operand/ALU path, which is now the only thing on the critical-path list.

  u_alu, 2 LUT levels                                  ~2.75 ns
  u_ex result/alu_result mux, 3 LUT levels (n701_*)    ~3.35 ns
  dmem address hold mux (dmem_addr_c_*)                ~1.47 ns

hypothesis.hypothesis:
This is purely a timing change. The cycle count must stay identical to the
champion (same stalls, forwarding and prediction), so all of the gain is Fmax.

1. Regfile off the BSRAM (rtl/reg_file.sv, rtl/id_stage.sv). Put
   (* syn_ramstyle = "distributed_ram" *) on `regs` so it maps to Gowin
   LUT-RAM (RAM16SDP4, async read). Keep the explicit write-first bypass and
   the x0 mux in reg_file. ID/EX rs1_val/rs2_val then become real fabric
   flops (tC2Q ~0.4 ns instead of 2.26 ns, and no s17/s16 LUTs after them).
   If Gowin still infers a BSRAM (check "BSRAM" in the timing summary: it
   should drop from 6 to 4, the 4 dmem byte lanes), use
   syn_ramstyle = "registers" instead. Area is not scored.
   The regfile read moves fully into the ID cycle
   (imem LFSR -> rs addr -> LUT-RAM -> bypass -> flop, ~7-8 ns), which is
   far off the critical path. Expected saving: ~3.4 ns on every
   u_rf-sourced path.

2. Registered forwarding selects (rtl/forward_unit.sv, rtl/core.sv,
   rtl/ex_stage.sv). Replace the combinational EX-stage compare with a
   2-bit select register per operand: 00 = ID/EX value,
   01 = EX/MEM.alu_result, 10 = MEM/WB.alu_result, 11 = MEM/WB.read_data.
   The wb mem_to_reg mux is folded into the select, so the EX operand is a
   plain 4:1 mux of four flops (LUT4 pair + MUX2_LUT5, about 1 level).
   The select is computed one cycle early by applying the existing
   priority function (EX/MEM > MEM/WB > none, rd != 0, reg_write) to the
   NEXT-STATE (D-input) values of the registers it reads. That makes it
   exact by construction:
     rs_addr_n   = stall_id ? id_ex.rsX_addr : if_id.instr[..]
                   (flush_id is deliberately ignored: a flushed entry has
                   ctrl=0/valid=0 and never becomes valid again, so its
                   select is a don't-care. This keeps the late redirect
                   out of the select cone.)
     exmem_rd_n  = stall_ex_mem ? ex_mem.rd : id_ex.rd
     exmem_we_n  = stall_ex_mem ? ex_mem.ctrl.reg_write
                 : (id_ex.ctrl.reg_write && !m_stall && !misalign_jump)
                   (branches never write, so misalign_jump is the only
                   trap term that matters. For JALR it needs only
                   jalr_sum[1], a 2-bit add of forwarded rs1[1:0] and
                   imm[1:0].)
     memwb_rd_n  = hold_mem_wb ? mem_wb.rd : ex_mem.rd
     memwb_we_n  = hold_mem_wb ? mem_wb.ctrl.reg_write
                 : (ex_mem.ctrl.reg_write && !mem_misalign)
     memwb_ld_n  = hold_mem_wb ? mem_wb.ctrl.mem_to_reg : ex_mem.ctrl.mem_to_reg
   Reset clears the selects to 00, which matches the all-zero reset of the
   pipeline registers. This removes the MEM/WB.rd/EX/MEM.rd -> compare path
   class (-11.44 ns) and turns the 3-LUT mux into ~1 level. Expected saving:
   ~1.5 ns.

3. Fold AUIPC's pc operand into ID (rtl/id_stage.sv, rtl/ex_stage.sv).
   The ID/EX rs1_val D-input becomes is_auipc ? pc : rf_rs1_data. The
   forwarding address used for the select is forced to 0 for AUIPC (also
   LUI/JAL, whose bits 19:15 are immediate), so the select is always 00.
   EX then uses alu_a = rs1 directly, and the post-forward alu_a mux and
   its 1.1 ns route disappear. RVFI-only fix-up: for AUIPC/LUI/JAL, report
   rvfi_rs1_addr = 0 and rvfi_rs1_rdata = 0 (their riscv-formal spec does
   not use rs1), so the reg/insn checks stay consistent.
   Expected saving: ~1.5 ns.

4. Dedicated dmem address generator plus a shorter result tail
   (rtl/ex_stage.sv, rtl/mem_stage.sv, rtl/core_pkg.sv).
   - Add an EX/MEM mem_addr field = rs1 + imm, from its own adder that
     takes the post-forward rs1 directly and has no op mux. mem_stage
     uses in.mem_addr for dmem_addr, byte masks, misalign and the RVFI
     aligned_addr. This is the register Gowin absorbs into the dmem BSRAM
     address, so the BSRAM path no longer goes through the ALU op mux,
     the link/muldiv mux or the shifter. alu_result stays for register
     writeback and forwarding.
   - Pre-merge the non-ALU writeback sources off the critical path:
     other = is_muldiv ? m_result : (pc+4). Both come from flops and an
     early adder. alu_result then goes through a single 2:1 after the ALU
     (sel_other decoded in ID and registered).
   Expected saving: 2-3 ns on the dmem path. The ALU -> alu_result flop
   path loses the hold mux and the BSRAM route (~2.5 ns).

Net estimate: ~16.4 ns -> ~12-12.5 ns on the current worst path class.
Other paths will then limit, probably the fwd -> branch compare ->
redirect -> PC path, which shrinks by the same ~5 ns of operand-side
savings from items 1-3. Realistic Fmax is 72-80 MHz (+16-29%) at
unchanged CoreMark cycles (4,382,792).

title: Rebuild the EX operand network: LUT-RAM regfile + fabric ID/EX operands, ID-precomputed one-hot bypass, dedicated AGU
motivation:
`make timing TARGET=bench` on the champion (place option 0, 60.7 MHz)
gives this worst path:
  cpu/u_rf/regs_regs_0_0_s -> dmem_0 BSRAM, 16.4 ns data, 13 cells.
Timeline of that path:
  - The register file is inferred as a BSRAM, whose output register IS
    ID/EX.rs1_val. BSRAM tC2Q = 2.26 ns (a fabric flop is about 0.4).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure where the operand decisions happen. The cycle behaviour
stays identical to the champion: same stages, the same distance-1/2
forwarding, the same load-use bubble, redirect timing, predictor and
M-unit handshake. CoreMark cycles should stay at about 4.38M.

1. Regfile as distributed LUT-RAM, with the operand register in the
   fabric.
   Rewrite reg_file.sv as a 32x32 array with two async read ports:
     - no reset loop (initial zeroing for sim is fine);
     - add (* syn_ramstyle = "distributed_ram" *) or the Gowin
       equivalent;
     - keep the write-first bypass and x0 handling combinational.
   id_stage then registers the fully bypassed value into fabric ID/EX
   flops. Every EX path then starts at a fabric FF (~0.4 ns instead of
   2.26 ns). The 2 bypass LUTs move into ID, where their inputs are
   early: the fetch word (LFSR/BRAM register), MEM/WB.rd, and the wb
   data.
   Confirm in the Gowin report that regs_regs_* are no longer BSRAM
   (the LUT-RAM count rises and BSRAM drops from 6 to 4).

2. Forward selects precomputed in ID and registered one-hot in ID/EX.
   ID compares its decoded rs1/rs2 fields:
     - against ID/EX.rd with ctrl.reg_write && rd != 0: next cycle's
       EX/MEM source, sel_x;
     - against EX/MEM.rd with reg_write && rd != 0: next cycle's
       MEM/WB source, sel_w, only when sel_x is false.
   These are the same distance-1/2 cases forward_unit handles today,
   one cycle earlier.
   sel_rf (use the register value) is the complement of those two.
   Its register is captured with the operand, and it is clear for
   x0 / LUI.
   EX gates the sel_x leg with the live ex_mem.ctrl.reg_write, which
   EX clears on a misaligned JAL/JALR trap. EX gates the sel_w leg
   with the live mem_wb.ctrl.reg_write, which the MEM misalign trap
   clears. That is one extra LUT input each.
   These selects stay correct under every stall because of how each
   stall moves the registers:
     - load-use flushes ID/EX, and the consumer re-evaluates in ID
       next cycle against the load in EX/MEM;
     - dmem_stall holds ID/EX and EX/MEM together, and MEM/WB keeps
       its data (hold_wb);
     - m_stall only holds the M-op itself, whose operands muldiv
       latches on its first EX cycle;
     - the instruction behind an M-op is captured on the done cycle,
       when EX/MEM holds a bubble;
     - a redirect kills the ID instruction.
   forward_unit's EX-side compare disappears.

3. One-hot AND-OR operand muxes with pc and imm folded in.
   MEM/WB carries one pre-muxed wb_data (mem_to_reg ? load_data :
   alu_result), selected in mem_stage before the register. It serves
   as both the WB write data and the MEM/WB bypass source. ID also
   registers one-hot sel_pc_a (AUIPC, JAL/JALR link), sel_imm_b
   (alu_src) and a 'four' bit for the link. The EX operands become:
     alu_a = sel_x_a&EXMEM | sel_w_a&WB | sel_rf_a&rs1_q | sel_pc_a&pc_q
     alu_b = sel_x_b&EXMEM | sel_w_b&WB | sel_rf_b&rs2_q | sel_imm_b&imm_q | four
   LUI falls out as 0 + imm, and JAL/JALR link as pc + 4 through the
   ALU adder. The EX/MEM result mux therefore loses its is_jump leg
   and keeps only the ALU vs the registered muldiv result.
   A separate 3-source rs1/rs2 AND-OR (exmem, wb, rf) feeds the branch
   comparator, the store data and muldiv. It uses the same registered
   selects without the pc/imm legs.
   Each operand is about 2 LUT levels from flops, down from about 6
   plus the BSRAM tC2Q.

4. Dedicated AGU plus a separate mem_addr register.
   agu = rs1_byp + imm_q (loads, stores, JALR target and its misalign
   bit; this replaces jalr_sum). It is registered into a new
   ex_mem.mem_addr. That field alone drives io_dmemAddr, the byte
   lanes, misalign detection, load alignment and the RVFI mem_addr.
   The ALU op-mux and result mux thus leave the BSRAM-address path.
   This matters because that path and the ALU -> alu_result path are
   currently at parity (-11.463 vs -11.449 ns).

- The shared operand prefix shrinks from about 8.5 ns to about 2.5-3 ns.
- The limit moves to the ALU op-mux path, the IF pre-decode/adder,
  the redirect/stall fan-out, or the ID LUT-RAM path, at about
  75-80 MHz (from 62.0).
- Cycles are unchanged, so fitness gains about +20% (roughly 170).
- Area: about +150-250 LUT for the 2x32x32 LUT-RAM, which frees 2
  BSRAM. About +70 flops (pc/imm/select bits already partly in
  ID/EX). Removed: jalr_sum, the EX comparators and the WB mux.

title: Predictor-steered run-ahead fetch: 2-entry fetch queue fills during back-end stalls to hide imem stalls; PC advance decoupled from hazard stalls
motivation:
The r2s2 champion already predicts in IF with zero bubbles. EX redirects
combinationally into the PC, so a mispredict or JALR costs only 1 bubble.
The remaining control-flow penalty is roughly 5-8K mispredicts + JALRs per
iteration out of about 438K cycles, i.e. about 2% of cycles. So no
direction-predictor refinement (gshare, a bigger BHT, a RAS) can clear the
4.6% acceptance bar.
The largest remaining overhead is imem backpressure. About 22% of fetch
cycles stall, costing about 0.28 CPI of the ~1.61 total. The fetch
bandwidth that could cover it is wasted: on every back-end stall cycle
(dmem stall, load-use bubble, MUL wait; roughly 45-50K cycles per
iteration) the PC holds and the word on the bus is thrown away, then
re-fetched and exposed to a fresh 22% stall. bench_stall_gen is a pure
function of the cycle count, so fetching during those cycles is free.
Because the predictor already steers the fetch PC through predicted-taken
branches and JALs, the front end can safely run ahead of decode.
A cycle-level Monte Carlo model uses the exact xorshift imem/dmem ready
sequence plus synthetic load/store (30-38%), load-use (4-10%), MUL and
redirect (2-5%) rates. It gives these cycle reductions:
  - 1 entry, consume-aware refill: 5.1-7.5%.
  - 2 entries, fetch gated only by registered occupancy (count < 2): 6.8-8.1%.
  - 3 entries: 8.2-9.7%.
The real core has a higher CPI (1.61) than the model (1.48-1.53). It
therefore has more back-end stall cycles to bank into, so the gain is at
the upper end.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Decouple fetch from decode with a 2-entry, predictor-steered fetch queue
that has a bypass.

1. if_stage.sv
   - `pc` becomes a run-ahead fetch_pc. The existing pre-decode and
     agree-BHT prediction are computed exactly as today from imem_data and
     fetch_pc (is_jal/is_br, imm, pred_target adder, BHT read at
     fetch_pc[7:2], misalign and 1 MiB guards).
   - fetch_ok = imem_ready && (count_q != 2). count_q is the registered
     occupancy. fetch_ok is deliberately independent of this cycle's
     decode stall and hazard signals.
     PC update priority: reset > redirect (pc <= redirect_target) >
     fetch_ok (pc <= pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4) > hold.
     This removes the load-use/dmem/m_stall -> stall_if -> PC-enable
     chain from the PC register entirely. That chain was part of the
     earlier u_ex->u_hazard->u_if critical paths.
   - Queue: 2 entries of {pc[31:0], instr[31:0], pred_taken, pred_ctr[1:0]}
     in plain flops (a shift FIFO: entry0 = head), plus count_q[1:0].
     Decode view (the IF->ID bundle):
       count_q != 0 : out = entry0, valid = 1
       count_q == 0 : out = {fetch_pc, imem_data, pred bits}, valid =
                      imem_ready (NOP 0x13 with valid=0 when not ready,
                      as today's flush_if does).
   - consume = decode-view valid && ID/EX captures it, i.e. !stall_id &&
     !flush_id && !redirect. This is an input from core.sv/hazard_unit.
     Update rules:
       redirect             : count <= 0 (queue flushed; the wrong-path
                               decode word and any fetch are dropped)
       count==0             : if fetch_ok && !consume -> entry0 <= fetched,
                               count <= 1 (bank the stalled word). If
                               consumed via bypass, count stays 0.
       count>=1             : head leaves on consume (entry0 <= entry1).
                               The fetched word (if fetch_ok) is appended
                               at the new tail. count <= count - consume
                               + fetch_ok.
   - pred_ctr and pred_taken travel with each entry. The EX/MEM-driven BHT
     update and the EX mispredict/agree logic are unchanged.
2. hazard_unit.sv / core.sv
   - Load-use compares ID/EX.rd against the decode-view rs1/rs2
     (if_id_w.instr[19:15]/[24:20]; entry0 when the queue is non-empty,
     else raw imem_data) instead of the raw io_imemData bits. This adds
     one 2:1 mux level on that compare. The mux select count_q!=0 is a
     register.
   - stall_id / flush_id / stall_ex_mem / hold_mem_wb equations are
     unchanged. stall_if and flush_if are replaced by the queue's own
     fetch_ok / decode-view valid. Export consume
     (= !stall_id && !flush_id) to if_stage.
3. id_stage.sv is unchanged. It already latches pc/instr/valid/pred bits
   from the IF->ID bundle.

Why it helps: each fetch that succeeds while decode is blocked banks one
instruction. The queue only drains on an imem-stall cycle, when decode
consumes the head with nothing fetched. So every banked instruction later
hides one imem-stall cycle, unless a redirect (about 1 per 35-50
instructions) flushes it first. imem stalls come about every 4.5
instructions, so nearly all banked entries get used.
Expected result is about 7% fewer cycles.
Fmax: the regfile-read -> fwd -> ALU -> dmem-address critical path
(21.8 ns) is untouched. The PC-enable cone shrinks. The decode/load-use
cone gains one mux level, which is well short of critical.
Cost is about 140 flops plus ~100 LUT4.

changes.description: Turn the PC into a run-ahead fetch_pc, steered by the unchanged pre-decode/agree-BHT prediction. Add a 2-entry shift-FIFO fetch queue of {pc, instr, pred_taken, pred_ctr} with registered count. fetch_ok = imem_ready && count != 2 is independent of decode stalls. The fetched word bypasses to decode when the queue is empty. Bank the word when decode does not consume it. Redirect flushes the queue and loads the target. The IF->ID bundle is the decode view (queue head or bypassed word; NOP/valid=0 when empty and imem not ready). Takes a new `consume` input instead of stall/flush.

Remove stall_if/flush_if; PC advance is now governed by the queue. Keep the stall_id/flush_id/stall_ex_mem/hold_mem_wb equations. Load-use compares against the decode-view rs1/rs2 inputs. imem_ready is no longer needed here.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-003-r3s2 (regression, +2.95%): The predictor-steered run-ahead fetch queue (2 flop entries plus a bypass; fetch gated only by the registered count_q != 2; the head is consumed on hazard_unit's id_advance, so dmem/load-use/MUL stall cycles bank imem words that later hide imem-stall cycles) cut cycles by ~6.4% (~4.38M -> ~4.10M, inferred from fitness/Fmax), just under the Monte Carlo model's 6.8-8.1% for 2 entries, but it cost ~3.6% Fmax (62.0 -> 59.8 MHz, +136 FF, +182 LUT4) for a net of only +2.95%, and the "regression" label means it lost to the same-round operand-path sibling r3s1 (201.34 at 88.2 MHz); hiding imem stalls is an IPC lever independent of that rebuild, so it is worth porting onto r3s1, but to clear the 4.6% acceptance bar with that ~6.8% speedup (1/0.936) the queue must cost under ~2% Fmax at ~88 MHz.

title: Flatten both co-critical EX tails: registered one-hot ALU result selects plus a one-LUT redirect, with flush removed from the ID/EX data-flop CE
motivation:
I ran `make timing` on the champion (r3s1, 201.34 at 88.2 MHz median;
this run used placement option 0, 79.6 MHz). Two independent path
families tie within 36 ps. Fixing only one of them gains nothing.

(A) Redirect cone, 17.858 ns, 13 levels:
ID/EX.b_x -> alu_b AND-OR (2 LUT, 2.7 ns) -> compare carry chain
(2.8 ns) -> branch_taken_s14/s5/s1 (3 LUT, 3.1 ns) -> redirect (1.5 ns)
-> flush_id (fanout 149, 1.1 ns) -> CE of ID/EX.pc (1.1 ns route).
The same cone ends at u_if/pc_* at 17.85 ns. The ID/EX always_ff is
`if (flush) {ctrl,valid,pred} else if (!stall) {all}`, so every ID/EX
data flop has CE = !flush && !stall. That is the same late-redirect CE
fanout that lesson r2s0 found worth +39% to remove.

(B) ALU result, 17.822 ns, 8 levels: ID/EX.ctrl.alu_op[4] -> seven
LUT levels that decode the 5-bit encoded alu_op and mux the result
(fanouts 18/12/8, 8.6 ns of routing) -> EX/MEM.alu_result. After that
come the is_muldiv ? m_result : alu_result mux and the 11-way `case`.
Lesson r3s1 showed that registered one-hot operand selects paid off.
The result side was never given the same treatment.

ID/EX.b_x -> alu_b AND-OR (2 LUT, 2.7 ns) -> compare carry chain
(2.8 ns) -> branch_taken_s14/s5/s1 (3 LUT, 3.1 ns) -> redirect (1.5 ns)
-> flush_id (fanout 149, 1.1 ns) -> CE of ID/EX.pc (1.1 ns route).
The same cone ends at u_if/pc_* at 17.85 ns. The ID/EX always_ff is
`if (flush) {ctrl,valid,pred} else if (!stall) {all}`, so every ID/EX
data flop has CE = !flush && !stall. That is the same late-redirect CE
fanout that lesson r2s0 found worth +39% to remove.

(B) ALU result, 17.822 ns, 8 levels: ID/EX.ctrl.alu_op[4] -> seven
LUT levels that decode the 5-bit encoded alu_op and mux the result
(fanouts 18/12/8, 8.6 ns of routing) -> EX/MEM.alu_result. After that
come the is_muldiv ? m_result : alu_result mux and the 11-way `case`.
Lesson r3s1 showed that registered one-hot operand selects paid off.
The result side was never given the same treatment.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
An IPC-neutral micro-optimisation of both co-critical EX tails. The
cycle count stays exactly 4,382,792.

1. ALU result selects become registered one-hot bits computed in ID
   from the decoded alu_op/is_muldiv:
     sel_add (ADD/SUB/LUI/AUIPC/JAL-link/other adder uses), sub
     lop[1:0] (00 = 0, 01 = AND, 10 = OR, 11 = XOR; this gates the
     logic leg inside one LUT4)
     sel_sll, sel_sr, sra
     sel_slt, sgn (SLT/SLTI and BLT/BGE)
     sel_md (M-op)
   EX then computes
     res = sel_add&sum | logic(lop) | sel_sll&sll | sel_sr&sr
         | {31'b0, sel_slt&lt} | sel_md&m_result
   as one AND-OR, about 2 LUT levels after the slowest unit, with no
   op decode on the path. The muldiv leg is folded in, so the separate
   is_muldiv result mux disappears. LUI keeps working as 0+imm through
   sum.
2. There is one shared comparator: ltu = alu_a < alu_b (a single carry
   chain) and eq = alu_a == alu_b. Signed less-than is
   ltu ^ (sgn & (a[31]^b[31])), and the sign term comes from the early
   operand bits. This feeds both SLT/SLTU and the branch unit. The
   separate signed/unsigned/eq/ge chains go away.
3. The static parts of the redirect are registered in ID:
     force = JALR | (JAL & !pred_taken)
     br    = is_branch & !instr[8]   (pc is 4-aligned, so
             branch_target[1:0] == imm[1:0]; this replaces the
             misalign_branch adder tap on the redirect path)
     is_eq = BEQ/BNE
     flip  = (BNE|BGE|BGEU) ^ pred_taken
   EX computes
     redirect = force | (br & ((is_eq ? eq : lt_eff) ^ flip))
   which is one LUT plus a MUX2_LUT5 after the chain, instead of five
   LUT levels. The non-JALR tgt_seq (pred_taken | imm[1]) is
   registered too. redirect_target for branches/JAL is then built only
   from pc+4 / pc+imm flop adders, which are early, and only the JALR
   AGU leg is late.
4. The ID/EX data fields load on `!stall` only, with no sync reset and
   no flush term. Flush/reset clear only valid, ctrl, pred_taken,
   pred_ctr, force and br (about 35 flops instead of about 250). This
   is safe:
   - load-use always has stall=1, so the data holds;
   - a redirect together with dmem_stall is still a hold;
   - an M-op in EX never redirects;
   - a valid=0/ctrl=0 entry feeds nothing, because forward selects,
     load-use, muldiv start, the BHT and RVFI are all gated by
     ctrl/valid.

- Family A goes from arrival 17.86 to about 14.0 ns: chain end
  -> 1-2 LUTs -> PC mux / 35 flops.
- Family B goes to about 13.5-14 ns: alu_b -> shifter (3 levels)
  -> 2-level AND-OR.
- The next limiter is expected to be the IF pre-decode path (imem
  BSRAM -> pc+imm -> pred_taken -> next_pc -> PC), estimated at
  about 98-102 MHz.
- Expected result: +10% or more on the median Fmax at unchanged
  cycles.

title: Registered branch resolution with EX squash bit plus ID-registered one-hot ALU result selects: cut both co-critical EX endpoints
motivation:
`make timing TARGET=bench` on the champion r3s1 (place option 0,
79.6 MHz; median 88.2) shows two co-critical path families.

(1) Redirect family (slack -7.563, 36 cells, fills paths 1-8 and
10-25 of the top 25). The chain is:
  - ID/EX.b_x;
  - alu_b AND-OR (2 LUTs, fanout 39);
  - the 32-cell branch-compare carry chain;
  - branch_taken_s14/s5/s1 (3 LUTs of branch_op mux);
  - redirect_Z_s (fanout 36);
  - u_id/n1462_s1: the flush/CE term, fanout 149;
  - the CE of ID/EX.pc_* and of IF pc_*.
The last 2 LUTs plus 2 high-fanout nets after branch_taken cost
about 2.8 ns of the 12.5 ns data path. They exist only because the
redirect is combinational into the PC mux and the ID/EX data-flop
enables.

(2) ALU result family (path 9, slack -7.528, only 35 ps behind). The
chain is:
  - ID/EX.ctrl.alu_op_4;
  - 8 LUT levels: n1304_s15 (fanout 18), n1295_s5 (fanout 12),
    n1309_s2 (fanout 8), then 4 single-fanout LUTs;
  - EX/MEM.alu_result_22.
This is the encoded 5-bit alu_op being decoded in EX, then the
11-way case mux with shifter / SLT legs, 68% of it routing.

Fixing either family alone buys only about 35 ps, so both must go
together. Lessons:
  - r2s1 lost with a registered redirect only because it also
    dropped the zero-bubble IF predictor.
  - The r2s2 IF agree-BHT is kept here, so only true mispredicts and
    JALRs pay the extra bubble: about 5-8K per iteration of about
    438K cycles, i.e. 1.2-1.8%.
  - r3s1 showed that turning EX-side decode into registered one-hot
    legs is worth about 5% Fmax on its own.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
A structural change to where branch resolution completes, plus moving
ALU result selection into ID. Stages, forwarding, the load-use bubble,
the IF predictor/BHT and the muldiv handshake are unchanged.

A. Registered redirect with a squash bit (ex_stage, hazard_unit,
   core, id_stage)
   1. EX computes redirect_fire exactly like today's `redirect`, gated
      with in.valid && !redirect_q.
   2. Register it:
        redirect_q <= redirect_fire && !dmem_stall
      so it fires once, on the cycle the branch/JALR leaves EX.
        redirect_tgt_q <= redirect_target
      Reset clears redirect_q.
   3. These flops drive the if_stage `redirect` / `redirect_target`
      (the PC takes redirect_tgt_q over any stall, as today). They
      also drive hazard_unit flush_id = (load_use | redirect_q) &
      !dmem_stall.
   4. Squash. When redirect_q=1, the ID/EX entry in EX is the first
      wrong-path instruction W1:
        - EX/MEM captures ctrl='0, valid=0 (reuse the m_stall bubble
          path in ctrl_with_trap);
        - is_mop is gated with !redirect_q, so muldiv never starts
          and m_stall=0;
        - its redirect is suppressed.
      EX/MEM then holds the branch, which is not a memory op, so
      dmem_stall=0 and the squash and flush always complete in that
      one cycle. A load-use against W1 is harmless: flush wins in
      id_stage and the redirect overrides stall_if. Gating load_use
      with !redirect_q is optional.
   5. Forwarding stays exact. The target T enters ID one cycle later.
      At that point:
        - ID/EX is a bubble (the flushed W2);
        - EX/MEM is a bubble (the squashed W1);
        - the branch is in MEM/WB, visible through the regfile
          write-first bypass.
      The BHT update from EX/MEM valid+is_branch never sees W1.
   6. id_stage: the ID/EX data-field CE becomes !stall only. Flush
      clears only valid/ctrl/pred bits; the data of a ctrl=0 entry is
      never consumed. This removes the 149-fanout flush net from the
      data flops.
   The redirect family now ends at a single flop D input, about 2.8 ns
   earlier. No EX-computed signal reaches the PC or the ID/EX enables
   any more.

B. ID-registered one-hot ALU result selects (id_stage, core_pkg,
   alu, ex_stage)
   1. Decode alu_op in ID into registered one-hot result-class bits
      in id_ex_t:
        - r_add (also covers LUI 0+imm and link pc+4);
        - r_sub;
        - r_slt, r_sltu;
        - r_xor, r_or, r_and;
        - r_sll, r_srl, r_sra (or r_shr + a registered arith fill bit).
   2. The ALU becomes an AND-OR of these legs:
        out = ({32{r_add}} & sum) | ({32{r_sub}} & diff) | ...
      This removes the 2-3 levels of EX-side op decode in path 9.
   3. Keep separate add and sub results, or one adder with a
      registered sub bit, whichever the implementer measures faster.
      The shifter's direction/arith controls also come from registered
      bits.
   4. Keep alu_op in ctrl for muldiv. The ALTOPS/real muldiv branches
      are untouched.

Cycle cost: +1 bubble per mispredict/JALR/unpredicted JAL, about
+1.2-1.8% (4.38M -> about 4.45M cycles).
Fmax: both co-critical families lose about 2-3 ns of their 12.5 ns
data paths. The next limiter should be the operand AND-OR ->
adder/shifter -> EX/MEM loop, or the fetch-word -> regfile/load-use
paths. Expect about 88 -> 98-102 MHz, a net gain of about +10%.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-002-r4s1 (improvement, +11.40%): Registering the EX redirect (redirect_q/redirect_tgt_q drive the IF PC and flush_id one cycle late, and redirect_q turns the wrong-path entry then in EX into an EX/MEM bubble, with is_mop gated so muldiv never starts), together with ID-registered one-hot ALU result selects (an AND-OR of r_add/r_sub/r_slt/.../r_shr legs, SRL/SRA sharing one shifter with fill r_sra & a[31]), lifted fitness 201.34 -> 224.29 and matched the +10% prediction (~99-100 MHz implied if the extra bubble per mispredict/JALR costs the estimated 1.2-1.8% of cycles; neither number was measured); unlike r2s1, it kept the zero-bubble IF agree-BHT so only true mispredicts pay the extra cycle, and the late squash needs no stall handling because the entry ahead of the wrong-path instruction in EX/MEM is the branch itself (not a memory op, so dmem_stall can't stretch it), so once a predictor keeps redirects rare, a registered redirect plus an EX squash bit is a cheap way to take every EX-computed signal off the PC mux and the ID/EX enables.

title: Predictor-steered 2-entry run-ahead fetch queue ported onto the one-hot-operand champion (redirect-free queue enables, flop-early PC enable)
motivation:
The champion (r3s1, 201.34, 88.2 MHz, ~4.38M cycles) already predicts in
IF with zero bubbles; a mispredict or JALR costs only 1 cycle. The
remaining control-flow loss is ~2% of cycles, so no direction-predictor
refinement (bigger BHT, gshare, RAS) can clear the 4.6% bar. The largest
remaining front-end loss is imem backpressure: ~22% of fetch cycles
stall, and on every back-end stall cycle (dmem stall, load-use bubble,
MUL/DIV wait) the PC holds and the fetched word is thrown away, then
re-fetched and exposed to a fresh stall.
r3s2 measured the fix on the older core: a predictor-steered 2-entry
fetch queue cut cycles 4.38M -> 4.10M (-6.4%, i.e. +6.8% fitness at
equal Fmax). It lost only against the same-round operand-network
rebuild; its critical path was still the old regfile-BSRAM -> dmem
path, not the queue. LESSONS: worth porting onto r3s1 if it costs
< ~2% Fmax at ~88 MHz.
Timing facts that decide the Fmax cost (checked with `make timing` in
this session):
  - Champion worst path: one-hot operand flop -> branch-compare carry
    chain -> redirect -> ID/EX flush/CE and the PC (36 cells). The imem
    word in the FPGA harness is an LFSR flop, so the fetch-word ->
    decode/regfile-address cone starts early and has slack.
  - Experiment: splitting ID/EX so the data flops load on !stall only
    (redirect off ~220 CEs) did NOT help: place option 0 gave 74.1 MHz
    vs the champion's 79.6 MHz, worst path now branch compare ->
    redirect -> PC / ID/EX ctrl. The limiter is the compare chain
    itself, not the fan-out. So that change is NOT part of this
    hypothesis, and the queue must simply not put anything new on the
    redirect cone.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Decouple fetch from decode with a 2-entry predictor-steered fetch queue,
built so that redirect only gains ~2 extra flop loads (the queue
count) and everything else the queue adds hangs off early signals.

1. if_stage.sv — run-ahead fetch PC + queue.
   - `pc` becomes fetch_pc. Pre-decode, pc+imm adder, agree-BHT read at
     fetch_pc[7:2], misalign and 1 MiB guards: unchanged, applied to
     the word being fetched (imem_data at fetch_pc).
   - fetch_ok = imem_ready && !full_q (full_q = registered count==2).
     PC update: reset > redirect (redirect_target) > fetch_ok
     (pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4) > hold. stall_if (load-use /
     dmem / m_stall) no longer reaches the PC: the fetch-word ->
     load-use compare -> stall_if -> PC-enable cone disappears and the
     PC enable becomes a flop-early signal. The redirect -> PC mux is
     exactly as today.
   - Queue: 2 flop entries {pc, instr, pred_taken, pred_ctr} as a shift

     one-hot empty_q (decode-view select).

title: Arrival-ordered tails: late carry-chain outputs enter only the last LUT on all three co-critical endpoints (ALU result, redirect_q, IF pc)

hypothesis.hypothesis:
IPC-neutral micro-optimisation. Every change keeps the exact
cycle-level behaviour of r4s1; cycles stay 4,442,763.

A. ALU result tail: the late leg enters last (alu.sv, ex_stage.sv,
   id_stage.sv, core_pkg.sv)
   1. Fold the muldiv result into the one-hot result select. Add a
      registered r_mul (= decoded M-op) to id_ex_t. The ID decode
      forces every r_* to 0 for M-ops, so r_add is no longer set by
      MUL. EX/MEM.alu_result D becomes the plain AND-OR, with no
      separate is_muldiv 2:1 mux after it.
   2. Split the AND-OR by arrival time:
        early = ({32{r_xor}} & (a^b)) | ({32{r_or}} & (a|b))
              | ({32{r_and}} & (a&b)) | ({32{r_mul}} & m_result);
        shift = ({32{r_sll}} & shl) | ({32{r_shr}} & shr);
        out   = (r_add ? sum : 0) | (r_sub ? diff : 0)
              | early | shift | {31'b0, slt_bit};
      Write it so that sum[i]/diff[i] go into ONE final LUT together
      with a pre-combined (early|shift)[i] net:
        out[i] = LUT4(sum[i], diff[i], other[i], r_sub_q)
      where:
        - other[i] is the OR of all non-adder legs;
        - the adder legs must be zeroed when r_add = r_sub = 0.
          Either use a registered r_as = r_add|r_sub and a LUT5
          (LUT4 x2 + MUX2_LUT5, which stays one level), or use one
          add/sub adder: a + (b ^ {32{r_sub}}) + r_sub, with the
          inversion folded into the alu_b operand LUT. The
          implementer picks whichever gives 1 level after the
          carry-chain SUM.
      Protect the structure from re-association:
        - put `/* synthesis syn_keep=1 */` on the `other` net, or
          make it a separate module instance;
        - check in the post-change timing report that at most 1-2
          LUTs follow the adder SUM.
      slt/sltu still use the chain MSB; they only feed bit 0.
B. Redirect tail: one LUT level after the compare (ex_stage.sv,
   id_stage.sv, core_pkg.sv)
   1. In ID, register the per-branch compare-kind bits:
        - br_eq (BEQ/BNE);
        - br_inv (BNE/BGE/BGEU);
        - br_sgn (BLT/BGE).
   2. In EX, form one lt value from a single chain, with the sign
      flip applied to operand bit 31 only (it enters at the chain
      end), plus the eq chain.
   3. Precompute the four early values v[eq,lt]. Each is:
        fire_u | (cond(eq,lt) ? fire_t : fire_n)
      evaluated for that constant eq/lt pair, using only registered
      or early bits.
   4. Then redirect_fire = v[{eq,lt}]: a 4:1 mux (LUT4 pair +
      MUX2_LUT5) directly in front of the redirect_q D input. That
      replaces branch_taken_s3/s1 + redirect_fire_s1/s0.
   branch_taken for EX/MEM (BHT update and pc_next) keeps its current
   logic; it ends at non-critical flops.
C. IF predict tail (if_stage.sv)
   1. Two adders:
        tgt_j = pc + imm_j;
        tgt_b = pc + imm_b;
      So the is_jal select moves from before the carry chain to after
      it. The fetch-word bits feed the adder inputs directly (no
      decode LUT and no 3.3 ns shared net in front of the chain).
   2. Decode is_jal / is_br locally in if_stage from imem_data[6:0].
      Stop Gowin from merging it with id_stage's b_four/opc decode:
      put syn_keep on if_stage's own decode nets, or duplicate the
      decode inside if_stage so no ID-side net drives IF.
   3. Build take_j and take_b as independent early/late terms:
        take_j = imem_ready & is_jal & !imem_data[21] & !tgt_j[20];
        take_b = imem_ready & is_br & dir & !imem_data[8] & !tgt_b[20];
      next_pc[i] is a single LUT:
        (tgt_j[i], tgt_b[i], pc4[i], take_j/take_b)
      with take_j/take_b one-hot.
   4. pred_taken is only registered into ID/EX. It no longer sits
      between the adder and the PC mux.
   5. Keep the stall/redirect priority. It is still 1 LUT (the
      existing n419_s0 level); stall and redirect are early
      registered/decoded signals.
D. Duplicate the high-fanout operand-select flops (id_stage.sv,
   ex_stage.sv)
   - b_x has fanout 32 with a 2.93 ns route; a_x/a_w/b_w and the
     other operand selects fan out similarly.
   - Register 4 copies of each operand-select bit (one per byte
     lane, each driving 8 bits of alu_a/alu_b/rs1/rs2).
   - Use syn_preserve=1 / syn_keep so Gowin does not merge the
     copies.
   This cuts the 2.9 ns select route to about 1 ns on both family A
   and family B.

Expected: every top-25 path loses about 1.5-3 ns of its 10.7 ns data
path. That is about 10.7 -> 9.3-9.6 ns, i.e. 92.7 -> ~105 MHz on
place option 0 and ~99.6 -> 107-110 MHz median, at identical
cycles. The next limiter is probably:
  - the operand AND-OR (2 LUTs) plus the adder chain alone;
  - or the dmem-BSRAM -> load-align -> MEM/WB.wb_data path.
Hence the moderate estimate: +8%.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-001-r5s0 (regression, -5.83%): Hand-ordering the EX result tail with syn_keep'd partial-OR nets (sum and diff from two separate adders entering only a final `r_sub ? diff : r_add ? sum : other` select), bundled with 4x byte-lane copies of the operand-select flops, a precomputed v[eq,lt] 4:1 redirect mux and dual pc+imm_j/pc+imm_b IF adders, scored 211.21 vs 224.29 (~94 vs ~99.6 MHz median implied if cycles are unchanged as designed, which was not confirmed; +8% was predicted); the only timing run was taken before the final early/other split (which was never timed) and gave 90.77 vs 92.7 MHz on option 0: wb_data -> alu_result was still 11 cells, because the barrel shifter arrives nearly as late as the carry chain and simply took the adder's place at the head of the kept 4-LUT `other` chain, and the 5-input final select (two adder outputs + other + two selects) mapped to 2 LUT levels, not 1, so the "only the adder leg is late" premise was false; since syn_keep locks in whatever partition you pick, read every leg's arrival time off the timing report before arrival-ordering a mux, keep the final select to <=4 inputs (e.g. one add/sub adder), and do not bundle four restructurings into one run, because then none of them can be credited or blamed.

title: Forward into the ID/EX operand registers: move the bypass mux to the end of the producer's cycle so EX operands are bare flops

hypothesis.hypothesis:
A structural change to where forwarding happens. The stages, the
predictor/BHT, the registered redirect + squash, the load-use bubble,
the muldiv handshake and all the stall rules stay as they are.
Forwarding moves out of EX and into the D-inputs of the ID/EX operand
registers. This is the "bypass into the operand latch" topology: the
consumer captures the producer's value as it is produced.

1. ID/EX carries four final operand values instead of the
   rs1_val/rs2_val + select bits:
     op_a : ALU operand a (rs1, pc, or 0 for LUI)
     op_b : ALU operand b (rs2, imm, or 4)
     src1 : raw rs1 (AGU base, RVFI)
     src2 : raw rs2 (store data, RVFI)
   In EX they are used as they are:
     alu_a = op_a, alu_b = op_b, rs1 = src1, rs2 = src2.
   There is no mux in front of the ALU, the branch compare, the AGU or
   muldiv.

2. Each operand's D-input in ID is a one-hot AND-OR. The x/w/r
   selects come from the same forward_unit compares as today (fetch
   word vs ID/EX.rd and EX/MEM.rd, both registered, x0 excluded,
   priority x > w > r). The legs are:
     x : ex_result, the combinational EX result of the instruction
         now in EX. It is the value that will be written to
         EX/MEM.alu_result this cycle.
     w : mem_wb_d, the combinational mem_stage wb_data (load-aligned
         or ALU) of the instruction now in EX/MEM. It is the value
         that will be written to MEM/WB.wb_data this cycle.
     early : the regfile read (write-first bypassed, so distance 3 is
         covered as today) plus the pc / imm / four / zero legs, all
         ANDed with their ID-decoded selects.
   To keep the late legs shallow, pre-merge
     t = (w & mem_wb_d) | early
   and put ex_result on the last LUT:
     d = (x & ex_result) | t
   That leaves 1 LUT level after the ALU result and 2 after the load
   data.

3. The capture is exact because of how ID/EX captures (unchanged):
   - A valid consumer enters ID/EX only when EX, EX/MEM and MEM/WB all
     advance: no dmem stall, no m_stall. Load-use and redirect flush
     it.
   - In that cycle the producer at distance 1 is finishing EX. For an
     M-op this is its done cycle, and ex_result carries m_result.
   - The producer at distance 2 is finishing MEM. If it is a load, a
     dmem stall would be holding ID/EX, so the data is valid.
   - A consumer held in ID/EX by a dmem stall or m_stall already has
     its operands. It no longer depends on MEM/WB keeping its data.
     hold_mem_wb can keep its current behaviour.
   - Stalled consumers still in ID re-evaluate their selects every
     cycle against the live ID/EX and EX/MEM contents, as they do
     today.
   - Wrong-path, squashed and trapping producers behave as today:
     - EX clears reg_write of a misaligned load/JAL/JALR before
       EX/MEM.
     - A misaligned load at distance 1 is covered by the load-use
       bubble.
     - A misaligned JAL/JALR at distance 1 fires redirect_q and
       squashes the consumer.
     - Squashed EX entries are bubbles with ctrl=0.

4. ex_result = alu_out | ({32{r_mul}} & m_result). r_mul is a new
   registered one-hot select (= is_muldiv). ID clears the other r_*
   bits for M-ops. This takes the separate muldiv 2:1 mux out of the
   loop, and EX/MEM.alu_result <= ex_result. The new loop is:
     op flop -> ALU -> result AND-OR -> 1 LUT -> op flop
   Today it is:
     fx/fw flop -> 2 LUT -> ALU -> result AND-OR -> 1 LUT -> alu_result
   Net gain: about 2 logic levels (-1.5 to -2 ns of about 10 ns).
   Branch compare -> redirect_q, AGU -> dmem address and muldiv
   operand latch each lose 2 levels too.

Risks the implementer must watch:
  - ex_result now fans out to 4 operand D-muxes plus EX/MEM.
  - mem_wb_d gains 2 levels after the dmem data.
  - The regfile leg gains 2 levels after the LUT-RAM read.
The fetch word comes from a flop in the timed harness, so the ID side
should have slack.
In fpga/core_bench_si.sv the dmem is a 2048-word async-read array.
Gowin maps it into BSRAM with EX/MEM.mem_addr absorbed as the address
register (about 2.3 ns clock-to-out). The w leg therefore adds 2
levels after roughly 4 levels of load alignment, which should still
fit within about 9 ns. Run `make timing TARGET=bench` and report the new
worst path. If the dmem -> mem_wb_d -> operand path turns critical,
the fallback is a hybrid: keep the w leg in EX as a single registered
(a_w & fw) OR term on top of the op flop, which is 1 LUT3, and keep
only the x leg and early legs in ID.

The change is IPC-neutral by design: cycles should stay at about
4.44M. The predicted Fmax is about 107-112 MHz, i.e. +7 to +12%.

lesson: - 2026-09-30 hyp-20260930-002-r5s1 (regression, +2.52%): Moving forwarding out of EX and into the ID/EX operand D-inputs (op_a/op_b/src1/src2 captured from a one-hot AND-OR of the live ex_result, the live mem_wb_d and pre-merged regfile/pc/imm legs, with the muldiv result folded into the ALU result AND-OR as an r_mul leg) removes about 2 LUT levels from the fw -> operand -> ALU -> alu_result loop on paper, but scored 229.94 vs 224.29 (~102 vs ~99.6 MHz implied if cycles stayed at ~4.44M, as designed but not confirmed) against the +7-12% predicted from r3s1/r4s1's "~5% per LUT level removed"; that is under the 4.6% acceptance margin and only ~1.3x the ~1.9% placement-option noise, hence the "regression" label, not a loss vs the champion; the bypass loop does not go away but closes through the operand D-mux instead, and the change adds paths the old design did not have (ex_result fanning out to four 32-bit D-muxes plus EX/MEM, dmem BSRAM -> load align -> mem_wb_d -> 2 LUTs -> operand flop, LUT-RAM regfile -> 2 LUTs), and no post-change timing report was captured to say which now limits Fmax, so per-level gains cannot be extrapolated across a restructuring that creates new paths, and this variant must be timed (with the hybrid that keeps the w leg as one registered AND term in EX tried if the dmem -> mem_wb_d path is the limiter) before anything is built on it.

title: Fetch from redirect_tgt_q in the redirect_q cycle: registered-redirect penalty 2 -> 1 bubble
motivation:
I ran the ISS (test/cosim/reference.py) over the timed CoreMark window
(2.92M instructions, about 4.44M cycles at the champion's IPC):
  - conditional branches 529.6K. The current 64x2 agree-BHT mispredicts
    46.3K of them (bimodal-1024: 39.5K, gshare-1024: 33.5K).
  - JALR 13.7K, every one of them exactly `ret` (0x00008067). The IF
    predictor never predicts a JALR, so all 13.7K redirect. A 4-entry
    RAS would hit 99.9% of them.
  - JAL 49.4K, already zero-bubble.
Since r4s1, each of the ~60K redirects costs 2 EX bubbles: the
wrong-path entry squashed in EX, plus the one ID/EX flushes while the
PC is only loading redirect_tgt_q. The second bubble is pure latency:
redirect_tgt_q is already a flop at the start of the redirect_q cycle,
so IF can fetch the target in that same cycle.
Gowin timing on the champion (make timing) shows three co-critical
families within 0.5% of each other:
  - the EX ALU tail (wb_data -> alu_result)
  - b_x -> branch compare -> redirect_q
  - lfsr (imem data) -> pre-decode -> pc+imm -> pc
A RAS needs a ret-verify compare feeding redirect_q (the second
family) to save only ~0.3% of cycles. A gshare/1024 BHT puts an XOR
and a deep LUT-RAM read on the IF cone to save ~0.3%. Both are
rejected. Cutting the redirect latency touches neither the EX
compare/ALU paths nor the late IF adder leg. It recovers most of what
r4s1's registered redirect cost, which is the largest predictor
lever left (a perfect predictor would only save ~2.7% of cycles).
